summary: The Certificate parameter in the Host Identity Protocol is a container for digital certificates carried in HIP control packets. This proposed standard specifies the parameter, the error signaling for failed verification, and how certain certificate types are represented in the DNS.

eli5.summary: Computers using HIP can show ID cards to each other. This defines the envelope where the ID card goes and what happens if it is bad.

questions: what is the hip cert parameter
how are hits used in x509 certificates
subtitle: A standard envelope for carrying digital certificates inside Host Identity Protocol control packets.

tldr.problem: Hosts using the Host Identity Protocol (HIP) derive their identity from a public key, but HIP had only a placeholder for sending certificates that vouch for those identities.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8002 defines the CERT parameter, a container that can hold a certificate or a pointer to one, with group and ID fields for ordered chains. It also defines two error signals and how a Host Identity Tag (HIT) appears in an X.509 v3 certificate.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 6253 by removing SPKI certificate support, and it updates RFC 7401. How certificates are obtained and acted on is left to the documents that use the parameter.

today: RFC 8002 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2016. It obsoletes RFC 6253 and updates RFC 7401, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why HIP Needs a Certificate Container
sections.content:
A digital certificate binds a piece of information to a public key by means of a digital signature. The holder of the matching private key can then make statements that anyone can check cryptographically.

The Host Identity Protocol (RFC 7401) defines a cryptographic namespace in which each host's identity is derived from a public key. Hosts can therefore sign data and issue certificates with their private key. RFC 8002 specifies the CERT parameter that carries such certificates in HIP packets. It fills a placeholder in Section 5.2 of RFC 7401, and so updates that RFC.

The RFC deliberately stays generic. Which certificates are used, how they are obtained or requested, and what happens after a successful or failed check depend on the scenario, so those details are left to the documents that use the parameter.
sections.eli5: HIP computers already have secret keys that prove who they are. This document gives them a standard envelope for passing around ID cards that other people have signed.

sections.title: The CERT Parameter
sections.content:
The CERT parameter is a container. It does not give certificates any meaning of its own. It is covered by the HIP SIGNATURE field and is a non-critical parameter. After the usual Type (768) and Length fields it carries four one-octet fields, then the certificate, then padding that makes the whole parameter a multiple of 8 bytes.

  • CERT group: an ID that ties related CERT parameters together.
  • CERT count: the total number of certificates in the group.
  • CERT ID: the sequence number of this certificate, counting from 1 up to the CERT count.
  • CERT type: what kind of certificate the parameter holds.

Padding bytes MUST be zeroed by the sender, and the receiver SHOULD NOT check their values. The certificates MUST use the signature and hash algorithms defined in RFC 7401.
sections.eli5: The envelope has little boxes on the front saying which pile the card belongs to, how many cards are in the pile, which number this one is, and what kind of card it is.

sections.title: CERT Groups and Certificate Types
sections.content:
A HIP control packet MAY contain several CERT parameters, each carrying one certificate. Related certificates form a CERT group that SHOULD be read in a set order, for example to express a certificate chain. A certificate with no relatives gets its own unique group number and a CERT count of 1.

A group MAY be split over several consecutive packets, but only if it does not fit in one. Inside a packet the CERT parameters MUST be in ascending order of CERT group, and a packet MUST NOT contain more than one incomplete group that continues in the next packet. The group and ID numbers are managed locally by each sending host.

Using the CERT parameter in the first Initiator packet (I1) is NOT RECOMMENDED, because it can slow the processing of I1s when a host is handling a storm of them.

Five type numbers are in use: 1 for X.509 v3, 3 for a hash and URL of an X.509 v3 certificate, 5 for an LDAP URL of an X.509 v3 certificate, and 7 for the Distinguished Name of an X.509 v3 certificate. Type 0 is reserved. The types 3, 5 and 7 give smaller packets than including the certificate, but the receiver must then fetch the certificate or check a local cache.
sections.eli5: If one ID card is not enough, you hand over a numbered stack, like page 1 of 3. You can also hand over just a note saying where to find the card, which is lighter to carry but means the other side has to go and look it up.

sections.title: Host Identity Tags in X.509 v3
sections.content:
RFC 8002 says how a Host Identity Tag (HIT) can appear in an X.509 v3 certificate. A HIT is written as an IPv6 address, as defined in RFC 7343, using the iPAddress form of the general name.

  • When the Host Identifier (HI) signs the certificate, its HIT SHOULD go in the Issuer Alternative Name extension.
  • When the certificate is issued for a HIP host, the host's HIT SHOULD go in the Subject Alternative Name extension, and the full HI is the subject's public key info.

The RFC also covers a managed PKI that knows nothing about HIP and cannot compute HITs. There the hosts send their identity certificates and the chain of intermediate CAs up to a root, or to a CA the peer trusts, as a CERT group. The peers validate each other's certificates and compute the peer HITs from the certificate public keys. Appendix A gives a full example certificate with encoded HITs.
sections.eli5: A HIP computer's name tag looks like an internet address. This document says which line of the ID card the name tag goes on, one line for who signed it and one for who it belongs to.

sections.title: Revocation and Error Signaling
sections.content:
Revocation follows Section 5 of RFC 5280 with two exceptions. Any HIP certificate serial number that appears on the Certificate Revocation List is treated as invalid whatever the reason code, and certificateHold is not supported.

Two HIP NOTIFY error types are defined:

  • CREDENTIALS_REQUIRED (48): the Responder will not set up an association because the Initiator did not send the credentials it needs. The Responder MAY send this.
  • INVALID_CERTIFICATE (50): sent after a certificate failed verification. Its notification data MAY hold the CERT group and CERT ID octets of the failing parameter.

Both signals are optional (MAY). A failed check does not require the verifier to say anything.
sections.eli5: If the bouncer needs a card you did not show, he can tell you that. If he looks at your card and it is fake, he can tell you which card in your stack was the problem.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Sending a group over several consecutive packets might allow attacks like those of IP fragmentation, such as sending pieces in the wrong order or skipping some to stall the victim and use up CPU or memory. Hosts SHOULD therefore implement a way to discard certificate groups with outstanding certificates when state space is scarce.

Putting a CERT parameter in an I1 is NOT RECOMMENDED, and the Initiator must keep in mind that the Responder can drop it without processing it. Checking the URL and LDAP types might let an attacker give the target bogus work (denial of service). Security considerations for X.509 v3 itself are in RFC 5280.
sections.eli5: Someone could start handing over a stack of cards and never finish, to keep you busy. So you are allowed to throw away half-finished stacks when you are running out of room.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 6253
sections.content:
RFC 8002 obsoletes RFC 6253. The only technical change listed is that support for SPKI (Simple Public Key Infrastructure) certificates has been removed. IANA obsoleted the type numbers 2, 4, 6 and 8, which had been the SPKI types, and updated the references in the "HIP Certificate Types" registry to this document.

New certificate types from the unassigned space are assigned through IETF Review. The RFC also defines two types in the "NOTIFY Message Types" subregistry.
sections.eli5: The old version also let you use a second kind of ID card. This version drops it, so those numbers are retired.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in octets, excluding Type, Length and Padding.

fields.name: CERT group
fields.desc: Group ID tying related CERT parameters together.

fields.name: CERT count
fields.desc: Total certificates sent, possibly over several packets.

fields.name: CERT ID
fields.desc: Sequence number of this certificate in the group.

items.label: Hash and URL of X.509 v3
items.desc: A hash and a URL pointing to the certificate.

items.label: LDAP URL of X.509 v3
items.desc: An LDAP URL pointing to the certificate.

items.label: Distinguished Name of X.509 v3
items.desc: The subject DN as a string.
